$comment: WHICH DECLARATION'S `nocommon`, THE ORDER THAT LINKS (P69 fold f26b, lane cs; the twin of examples/c/two_units_nocommon_on_the_later_tentative_declaration_refused). Each unit declares `int t __attribute__((nocommon));` and then `int t;`. This compiler reads the merge survivor's mark from the LAST tentative declaration (`settleNoCommon`), which states no `nocommon`, so each unit's `t` is a COMMON and the two are one object: main.c stores 40, other.c reads it, exit 42. THE SPLIT, decided for gcc's reading (probe rv cell 15 read the objects: a common on gcc 13.3.0 and mingw-w64 gcc 13.2.0, a `.bss` definition on clang 18.1.3). MEASURED 2026-10-20, lane cs probe nc (the two units compiled and linked in both orders, with and without `-fcommon`): gcc 13.3.0 on Linux x86_64 (report 20261020-113301-0bb1b5bb) and mingw-w64 gcc 13.2.0 (report 20261020-111822-cc9ed60f) link it under `-fcommon` and it exits 42 in both orders, and refuse it under their default `-fno-common` (two definitions); clang 18.1.3 (the same report) and Apple clang 21.0.0 (report 20261020-113411-30942175) refuse it with and without `-fcommon` — clang's reading, each `t` a definition. The CONTROL of that probe, both declarations in the OTHER order (the refusing twin's units), is refused by every one of them. This compiler's tentative definitions are commons on every format whose document states commons (cl's default, gcc's and clang's `-fcommon`), so the program runs on the four targets below; a document that states no commons is the refusing twin's business, not this program's.
